Men take wives because they are weary; women take husbands because they are inquisitive. Both find themselves disappointed.’

‘I doubt that I shall marry, Harry. I am too deeply in love. That is one of your maxims. I am following it, as I follow everything you tell me.’

‘With whom are you in love?’ Lord Henry asked after a moment.

‘An actress,’ Dorian Gray replied, colouring.

Lord Henry lifted his shoulders. ‘A somewhat ordinary beginning.’

‘You wouldn’t think so if you saw her, Harry.’

‘Who is the girl?’

‘She is called Sibyl Vane.’

‘I’ve never heard the name.’

‘Nobody has. One day they will, though. She has genius.’

‘My dear fellow, no woman possesses genius. Women are the ornamental sex. They have nothing to say, and deliver it delightfully. In women, matter triumphs over mind, just as in men, mind triumphs over morality.’

‘Harry, how can you say such a thing?’

‘My dear Dorian, it is perfectly true. I am studying women just now, and ought to be informed. It proves a less obscure subject than I had supposed. In the end I discover only two varieties: the plain and the painted. Plain women are exceedingly useful. To acquire a name for respectability, one need only escort them to supper. The others are exceedingly charming. They do, however, make a single mistake: they paint their faces in the hope of appearing young. Our grandmothers painted theirs in the hope of speaking brilliantly. Rouge once accompanied wit. Those days are finished. A woman is entirely content if she can appear ten years younger than her daughter. Where conversation is concerned, London contains only five women worth addressing, and two are inadmissible in respectable society. But tell me about this genius of yours. How long have you been acquainted?’

‘Oh, Harry! Your opinions frighten me.’

‘Never mind my opinions. How long have you known her?’

‘Some three weeks.’

‘And where did you find her?’

‘I shall tell you, Harry, only you must not be unkind about it. It would never have happened, after all, had I not met you. You awakened in me an extravagant longing to learn everything about life. For days following our meeting, I felt something pulsing through my veins. While idling in the park or wandering along Piccadilly, I would examine every passer-by, wondering with a feverish curiosity what kind of existence each one led. Some held me spellbound; others terrified me. A delicious poison seemed to hang in the air. I craved sensations....’

‘Story!’

He appeared deliberately to misunderstand the word she echoed, for he hurriedly continued, ‘Yes, customers. In banking we generally speak of those connected with us as our customers. He was a French gentleman, a man of science and considerable learning—a Doctor.’

‘Not from Beauvais?’

‘Indeed, from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, this gentleman came from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, he enjoyed a reputation in Paris. I had the honour of meeting him there. Our dealings were commercial, though confidential. At that period I was with our French House, where I had been for—oh, twenty years.’

‘At that period—might I ask what period you mean, sir?’

‘I mean twenty years ago, miss. He married an English lady, and I acted as one of the trustees. His affairs were wholly entrusted to Tellson’s, as were those of many French gentlemen and families. In much the same fashion, I am, or have been, a trustee in one capacity or another for scores of customers. These are strictly business connections, miss, involving neither friendship nor special concern nor anything resembling sentiment. Throughout my business life I have moved from one to the next, precisely as during my working day I move between our customers. To put it briefly, I possess no feelings; I am simply a machine. To continue—’

‘But, sir, this is my father’s story, and I am beginning to believe’—her oddly furrowed brow was turned intently toward him—‘that when my mother survived my father by only two years and left me an orphan, you were the person who brought me to England. I am nearly certain you were.’

Mr. Lorry took the small, uncertain hand that reached trustfully for his and lifted it to his lips with a degree of ceremony. He then led the young lady directly back to her chair. Grasping its back with his left hand, and employing his right alternately to stroke his chin, tug his wig beside his ears, or emphasize his remarks, he stood gazing down at her face while she gazed up at his.

‘Miss Manette, I was indeed that person. And you will understand how accurately I described myself when I said I had no feelings, and that my connections with other people were purely commercial, if you consider that I have not seen you since. No; all this time you have remained Tellson’s ward, while I have occupied myself with Tellson’s other concerns. Feelings! I have neither leisure nor opportunity for them. My entire life, miss, is spent turning a vast financial Mangle.’

In the days of my youth, discontent never entered my thoughts; and whenever weariness overtook me, a beautiful prospect in nature or the contemplation of excellence and sublimity in human works could invariably engage my heart and restore vigour to my spirits. But I am a tree struck by lightning: the thunderbolt has pierced my soul. I felt then that I should live on as an example of what I shall soon no longer be—a wretched image of ruined humanity, an object of pity to others and unbearable to myself.

We remained at Oxford for a considerable time, wandering through the surrounding country and seeking out every place connected with the most stirring period of English history. These modest expeditions were frequently lengthened by one object of interest succeeding another. We saw the grave of the celebrated Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a little while my soul rose above its abject and unhappy terrors to dwell upon the sacred principles of liberty and self-sacrifice, of which these places served as monuments and reminders. For one brief instant I ventured to cast off my fetters and survey the world with a proud and liberated spirit. Yet the iron had bitten into my flesh, and I relapsed, shivering and without hope, into my own miserable being.

We departed Oxford reluctantly and continued to Matlock, our next stopping-place. The landscape surrounding that village bore a closer likeness to Switzerland, although all its features were smaller. Its green hills lack the crown of remote, snow-white Alps that invariably rises beyond the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We explored the remarkable cavern and the small natural-history collections, whose curiosities were arranged in the same fashion as those at Servox and Chamounix. Hearing Henry speak the latter name made me shudder, and I was eager to leave Matlock, now linked in my mind with that dreadful scene.

After Derby, continuing north, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Here I could almost imagine myself amid the Swiss mountains. The small remnants of snow still clinging to the mountains’ northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing streams over rocks were sights both familiar and beloved. We also formed acquaintances there who came close to beguiling me into happiness. Clerval’s enjoyment surpassed mine in proportion: among talented men his mind unfolded, and he discovered powers and resources within himself greater than he could ever have supposed he possessed when his companions had been his inferiors.
